name: Nandi Hills

horizon_profile.description: Open sky to north, west, and east. Low hills block south-east below ~10°. Good for most observations.

access.night_access_notes: Road open 24 hours. Gate may close after 10 PM on weekdays — arrive early or confirm with local authorities.

notes: One of the most accessible dark-sky sites from Bangalore. Popular sunrise point — stargazers should arrive before crowds. Fog possible in winter post-midnight.

name: Skandagiri (Kalavara Durga)

horizon_profile.description: Summit offers near-360° open sky. Minor obstruction to the south from the ridge. Excellent for all-sky meteor watching.

access.night_access_notes: Night trek to summit required (~2 hours). Trekking permit needed — book via Karnataka Ecotourism. Not suitable for heavy telescope equipment.

notes: Best dark sky near Bangalore but requires a night trek. Carry all water and warm layers. Stunning for naked-eye and binocular observing. Not ideal if you need a telescope — carry weight is the constraint.

name: Coorg (Madikeri / Abbey Falls Road)

horizon_profile.description: Rolling hills with coffee plantations. Western horizon is open. Eastern horizon partially blocked by Western Ghats ridgeline below ~12°.

access.night_access_notes: Multiple homestays with open grounds suitable for telescope setup. Ghats roads can be foggy — drive carefully.

notes: Bortle 3 — one of the darkest accessible skies in southern Karnataka. Milky Way visible to the naked eye on clear nights. Leeches during monsoon. Best combined with a weekend homestay trip.

name: Horsley Hills

horizon_profile.description: Hilltop viewpoint with good sky coverage. South and south-west open. Some tree canopy obstruction on northern approaches.

access.night_access_notes: AP Tourism resort available. Roads well-maintained. Open access at night.

notes: Underrated dark-sky site. Less crowded than Nandi Hills. AP Tourism resort makes overnight stays comfortable. Good compromise between darkness and amenities.

name: Spiti Valley (Kibber / Langza)

horizon_profile.description: High-altitude cold desert with near-perfect 360° horizon. Minimal light pollution. One of the darkest skies in India.

access.night_access_notes: Accessible only May–October (Rohtang/Kunzum passes close in winter). Roads are rough. 4WD recommended. AMS risk above 3500m — acclimatize first.

notes: Bortle 1 — the gold standard. Milky Way casts shadows here. Altitude means thinner atmosphere and steadier seeing. But requires serious travel planning. Nights can drop to -10°C even in summer. Altitude sickness is a real risk — spend 2 days acclimatizing.

name: Rann of Kutch (White Desert)

horizon_profile.description: Perfectly flat salt desert — true 360° unobstructed horizon to ground level. No terrain interference whatsoever.

access.night_access_notes: Best during Rann Utsav (November–February). Permit required for border areas. Stay at tent cities or Dhordo resorts.

notes: Bortle 2 with an absolutely flat horizon — objects visible from the moment they rise. The white salt surface provides a surreal landscape under starlight. Extreme heat outside the winter window. Combine with Rann Utsav for a full experience.

name: Mahabaleshwar (Wilson Point / Arthur's Seat)

horizon_profile.description: Western Ghats escarpment. Excellent western horizon (overlooks Konkan plains). Eastern horizon partially limited by hills.

access.night_access_notes: Multiple hotels and resorts. Wilson Point has road access. Ghat roads — drive carefully at night.

notes: Best accessible dark sky from Mumbai/Pune corridor. Wilson Point at 1439m is the highest point — best for observation. Avoid monsoon season (extreme rainfall June–September). Fog common in late winter.

name: Savandurga (base area)

horizon_profile.description: Large monolithic hill blocks eastern sky below ~25°. Western, northern, and southern horizons are open and flat.

access.night_access_notes: Trekking to summit banned. Base area accessible by road. Multiple spots along approach road suitable for observation.

notes: Closest dark-ish sky from Bangalore. Bortle 5 is not ideal for deep sky but adequate for planets, bright clusters, and meteor showers. Good for a quick weeknight trip. Eastern sky severely limited by the hill — plan observations accordingly.

name: Hanle (Indian Astronomical Observatory)

horizon_profile.description: High-altitude plateau. Near-perfect 360° horizon. One of the world's best astronomical sites — home to India's highest optical telescope.

access.night_access_notes: Requires Inner Line Permit (apply via Leh DC office). Accessible June–September only. No public transport — self-drive or hired vehicle from Leh (~250 km, 10 hours). Severe AMS risk.

notes: Bortle 1 — possibly the darkest accessible sky in India. Home to the Indian Astronomical Observatory (2m Chandra telescope, GROWTH-India telescope). Professional-grade seeing conditions. But extremely remote — plan as a multi-day expedition. Nights drop well below 0°C even in summer.

name: Yelagiri Hills

horizon_profile.description: Valley surrounded by hills. Southern and western sky is open above ~10°. Northern horizon partially limited by hill ranges.

access.night_access_notes: 14 hairpin bends on the approach road — drive carefully at night. Multiple resorts available for overnight stays.

notes: Good dark-sky site accessible from both Bangalore and Chennai. Less crowded than Nandi Hills. The lake area offers open sky. Paragliding and trekking also available — can combine stargazing with other activities.
